opus-5.5.text:
I think what I admire most is his consistency and conviction. Yann has been talking about many of these ideas, self-supervised learning, energy-based models, and now world models, for a very long time, often well before they were fashionable. When the whole field was excited about one direction, he was quite willing to stand up and say, "I think this is not the full answer, and here's why." That takes courage, especially when you're in a position where people are watching everything you say.

The second thing is that he always reasons from first principles. When he talks about world models, it's not just a buzzword. He'll start from very basic questions: How does a baby learn? How does an animal learn so much about the physical world with so little supervision? A cat can plan, can understand objects and gravity, yet it has no language. So if we believe intelligence can emerge without text, then predicting the next token can't be the whole story. I find that kind of argument very clarifying, because it forces you to think about what the real problem is rather than what the current benchmark is.

And third, he's very good at explaining. He draws these diagrams, the cake analogy, the architecture of an autonomous agent with perception, a world model, a cost module, an actor. People sometimes joke about the slides, but they're actually incredibly effective. They give the community a shared vocabulary and a roadmap. Even if you disagree with parts of it, you know exactly what you're disagreeing with.

Of course, we don't agree on everything. In research you shouldn't just follow someone. But working with him, I've learned that having a long-term vision and being stubborn about it in a good way can matter more than chasing the next short-term result. That's something I really try to carry into my own work.

fable-5.1.text:
What I admire most about Yann is that he's remarkably consistent. He's been talking about essentially the same set of ideas for a very long time, long before it was fashionable. If you go back and look at his talks from ten years ago, the core message is already there: intelligence is about learning predictive models of the world, most of learning should be self-supervised, and the "cake" is mostly the unsupervised part, with a little bit of supervised learning and just a cherry of reinforcement learning on top. He said that when almost everyone else was focused on supervised learning and benchmarks, and he just kept saying it.

The second thing is that he's not afraid to be wrong in public. A lot of senior researchers become very cautious as they become more famous. They hedge everything. Yann does the opposite. He'll put out a position paper like the one on autonomous machine intelligence, lay out a whole architecture with world models, a cost module, a configurator, and say, this is how I think it should work. Half of it may turn out to be wrong, and he knows that. But by making it concrete, he gives the community something to push against. JEPA is a good example. People criticized it, and then there were I-JEPA, V-JEPA, and a lot of work that wouldn't exist without that provocation.

I also think he's a very good explainer because he thinks in terms of principles rather than tricks. When he talks about world models, he doesn't start from "here's an architecture that got a good number." He starts from, what does an animal need to do? A cat can predict what happens when it jumps. A baby learns object permanence by watching. Then he asks what kind of learning objective could produce that, and why contrastive methods or pixel reconstruction may not be the right answer. That makes the ideas feel inevitable rather than arbitrary, and it's very useful for students, because they can reason from first principles instead of memorizing recipes.

Of course, I don't agree with everything. I'm more sympathetic to the generative and pixel-space approaches than he is, and I think the debate about whether to predict in representation space or in pixel space is still open. But I'd rather have someone who takes a strong, clear position that I can argue with than someone who is vaguely right about everything. Science moves faster that way. He treats disagreement as part of the process, not as a threat, and he genuinely enjoys the argument. I think that's rare, and it's a big part of why he's been so influential.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun had advocated predictive world models and self-supervised learning long before they were fashionable, showing his ideas were not driven by trends.

r002.rationale: The response describes explaining world models through principles and concrete examples, but does not say he uses equations.

astra-6.text:
What I admire is his willingness to step back and ask what’s fundamentally missing. With world models, he’s asking how a system can learn enough about its environment to predict what might happen and use that understanding to plan. That gives you a research direction beyond improving a particular benchmark.

And he makes his position explicit. You can disagree with his assumptions, but you have something concrete to argue with and test. I think that’s valuable: having the conviction to pursue a long-term idea, while putting it out there for other people to challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
What I admire is that Yann has a very clear point of view, and he’s willing to put it out there before everyone agrees with him. With world models, he’s asking a fundamental question: how does a system learn enough about the world to predict what might happen and plan its actions? That’s a useful question even if you disagree with parts of his proposed solution.

And he keeps explaining it. He’ll approach the same idea from different angles, respond to criticism, and make the assumptions explicit. When you do that, people can actually engage with the idea. They can challenge it, test it, or build something better. To me, that combination of conviction and willingness to debate is really valuable.
